newsitem.title: JAPAN: JAPAN TRADERS SAY POLITICS LOOM LARGE IN IRAQI OIL.
newsitem.headline: JAPAN TRADERS SAY POLITICS LOOM LARGE IN IRAQI OIL.

text.p: Japanese oil refiners were worried on Thursday that talks between trading giant Mitsubishi Corp and Iraqi oil marketer State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) could be strained by political concerns, traders said.
"We have been notified by our head office that Baghdad has decided not to allocate to Japan in August," said a Singapore trader with a Japanese refiner that was also pursuing Iraqi barrels.
"This is not a decision between SOMO and Japan companies, but between the Iraqi government and Japan," a spokesman with the company said, asking that the company not be identified.

A trader with a separate refiner said that Japan would never be given preferential treatment in the oil sales because of its political alignment with the United States and its role as both a non-permanent member of the U.N. Security Council and a member of the U.N. Sanctions Committee.

"During the last round of sales, Russian and French companies, which have also been aggressive in offering upstream investment following the sanctions, had first access," he said. Japan companies as a whole are hoping to secure at least 40,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Iraqi exports.
Both Mitsubishi Corp, which is representing four Japan refiners, and Idemitsu Kosan Co Ltd have sent negotiators to Baghdad for oil talks.
Cosmo Oil Ltd has also said it is pursuing barrels, but has not sent negotiators to Baghdad.
None of the companies would officially comment on the negotiations, but most traders assume Japan will secure barrels for September.
"I don't think we will be left out completely if there are some barrels left for us, but we are not among the favourites," the trader with the refiner said.

Because U.N. trade sanctions imposed on Iraq bar international flights to and from Baghdad, the journey for traders travelling from Tokyo involves a 500 mile four-wheel drive trek from Amman, Jordan -- almost 10 hours across parched mountain and desert -- to the Iraqi capital.
An official from Iraq's embassy in Tokyo said he was unaware of any developments in the negotiations.

"Iraq has always declared its position that after the (United Nation) sanctions are lifted, we will give preference to the countries and companies which have helped Iraq and its citizens overcome the pain and difficulty imposed upon us by the sanctions," he said.
